e.etymology: A short form of Vanessa, a name Jonathan Swift coined in the 18th century from the name of his friend Esther Vanhomrigh. Nessa is also an old Irish name, borne by the mother of King Conchobar in legend.
namesakes: Nessa Barrett (singer who rose to fame on TikTok)

assoc.t: Nessarose, called Nessa, Elphaba's sister in Wicked

e.etymology: Anglicized from Scottish Gaelic Fionnlagh, fair warrior or fair hero, from fionn, fair, and laoch, warrior. Finlay is the usual spelling in Scotland; Finley is commoner in the US.
A modern Caribbean Spanish coinage in the family of Yaileen and Jailyn. Its 2022 peak in the US followed the rise of Dominican rapper Yailin La Más Viral.

assoc.t: Yailin La Más Viral, Dominican rapper

e.etymology: A modern elaboration of Eva or Evie with the -iana ending of names like Aviana and Liliana.
From Punjabi asis, a blessing, from Sanskrit ashis. It is used chiefly in Sikh families.
A pet form of Wilhelmina, Minerva, Mary and other names, formed with the -ie ending. It was popular as a full name in the 19th century and ranked among the top ten US girls' names in the 1880s.
namesakes: Minnie Driver (actress in Good Will Hunting)

e.etymology: An English surname from the medieval personal name Elwald, from Old English aelf, elf, and weald, rule.
namesakes: Elwood Blues (Dan Aykroyd's character in The Blues Brothers)
Elwood P. Dowd (James Stewart's character in Harvey)

assoc.t: Elwood Blues of The Blues Brothers

e.etymology: A 20th-century American spelling of Cory, a surname of uncertain origin that became a popular first name in the 1970s and 1980s.
A doubled Lu, the pet form of Louise, Louisa, Lucy and Lucille, used as a full name since the 1800s. In Arabic lulu means pearl, and Lulu is also a Chinese name made by repeating one syllable.
namesakes: Lulu (Scottish singer of To Sir with Love)

assoc.t: Lulu, common nickname for Lululemon activewear
a lulu, something remarkable or outrageous

e.etymology: A form of DeAndre, an African American coinage that adds the De- of DeShawn and DeAngelo to Andre. Andre is the French form of Andrew, from Greek andreios, manly.
From Italian novella, the feminine of novello, new or early, from Latin novus. The same word names a short novel.
Probably an anglicized form of Irish Odhrán, a saint's name formed from odhar, dun or sallow. It has also been taken as a variant of Hebrew Oren, pine tree.
namesakes: Orrin Hatch (US senator from Utah for 42 years)

e.etymology: In the US mostly a modern elaboration of Mark in the style of Markell and Martell. Markel is also the Basque form of Marcel, from Latin Marcellus, a diminutive of Marcus.
A transposed spelling of English John that became an established name in Colombia, Peru and Brazil. John comes from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
e.note: English speakers often take it for a misspelling of John.

e.etymology: The Polish and Catalan form of Anthony, from Latin Antonius, a Roman family name of unknown meaning.
namesakes: Antoni Gaudí (Catalan architect of the Sagrada Família)
Antoni Porowski (food expert on Queer Eye)

e.etymology: A spelling of Melody, the English word used as a name since the 20th century, from Greek melodia, singing. Melodi is also the Turkish form.
From Spanish milagro, miracle, probably shortened from Milagros, a name honoring the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of Miracles.
An English surname from any of several places named Prescot or Prescott, from Old English preost, priest, and cot, cottage.
namesakes: Prescott Bush (US senator, father of President George H. W. Bush)

e.etymology: A modern coinage that puts a Z on the sound of Tyler and Kyler.
The Ashkenazi pronunciation of Hebrew Binyamin, the Biblical Benjamin, from ben, son, and yamin, right hand. Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob.
A respelling of Boston, the Massachusetts city named for Boston in Lincolnshire, England, a place name traditionally explained as Saint Botolph's town.
The Greek form of Isaiah, from Hebrew Yeshayahu, Yahweh is salvation. The King James New Testament calls the prophet Esaias, and the form is traditional in Sweden and Finland.
A modern blend of Quinn and the -ley ending of Kinley and Finley. Quinley also exists as a surname.
A respelling of Harmony, the English word used as a name, from Greek harmonia, a fitting together or agreement, also the name of a Greek goddess of concord.

e.meaning: dweller by a bank or hillside
e.etymology: A respelling of Banks, an English surname for someone who lived beside a bank, a slope or riverside. The X follows Jax and Knox.

assoc.t: sounds like banks, the financial institutions

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Yolande, a medieval royal name of obscure, probably Germanic, origin. It has long been identified with Violante and with Greek ion, violet, and anthos, flower.
namesakes: Yolanda Hadid (reality TV star, mother of Gigi and Bella Hadid)

assoc.t: Yolanda Saldívar, who killed the singer Selena

e.etymology: An American spelling in the Aniyah and Anaya family, built on the -iyah ending that spread in the 2000s after Aaliyah.
A spelling of Jay, long a pet form of names beginning with J. Jae is also a common element of Korean given names, with a meaning that depends on the character chosen.
A spelling of Yaretzi, a name popular with Mexican American families since the 2000s. It is often said to be Nahuatl for you will always be loved, though that reading is not established.
The French word for thank you, from Latin merces, reward, the same root as English mercy. As a name it works as a French-flavored spelling of Mercy.
A Hebrew name from asah, to make, and El, God. In the Bible Asiel is a man of the tribe of Simeon named in 1 Chronicles.
